name: Felix Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Chemistry is the course, so I'm in lectures in the morning and in the lab three afternoons a week, wearing goggles that give me a mark on my nose. I live in a flat with three lads from halls and we have a rota for who buys the bin bags. Evenings I stack shelves at a supermarket three shifts a week. On the side, I edit short videos for a couple of local gyms, which pays better than the supermarket.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like making something change colour in a flask and knowing exactly why. I also like that I'm hustling a bit on the side. What wears me out is sleep, because I stay up editing, and the pile of maths that goes with chemistry. I use an AI model for nearly everything, from my lab report outlines to scripts for the gym videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it's a handy tool and it's already doing most of what it can do. I'd tell my gym clients that their videos will be better and faster, and I'd say it with a smile. The big doom stories are for people who don't try the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel fine. Chemistry's hands-on in the lab, and the tools I use now would just keep getting a bit better. My worry is the usual one, getting a lab job when I graduate. There aren't many nearby, so I'd have to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on everything. I'd carry on the shifts and the video work, and I'd start building a portfolio of lab skills and a short LinkedIn-style profile. I'd also learn a bit of Python for chemistry data, because it sets you apart. And I'd save about a third of my video money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Cheerful. It's the world I'm already in, and I like it. I'd get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there aren't many lab jobs nearby. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: You said there aren't many lab jobs nearby. Does that bother you?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the gym owners think of the videos?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yes. It means I'd have to move for the first job, which costs money and takes me away from my family. But I don't mind moving at all, and I think I'd enjoy it. I'd rather be somewhere with a good lab than stay in a town with no openings.

say: I'd say it's a **handy tool** and it's already doing most of what it can do.
I'd tell gym clients their videos get **better and faster**.
think: Chemistry is hands-on, and my tools would just keep getting **a bit better**.
My worry is the usual one: **few lab jobs** nearby, so I'd have to move.
do: **Keep** supermarket shifts and the gym video work.
**Learn** a bit of Python for chemistry data to stand out.
**Save** about a third of my video income.
feel: **Cheerful**, because it's the world I already live in.
S0.quote: I'd rather be somewhere with a good lab than stay in a town with no openings.
fieldNote: Felix is **comfortable** because he already uses the tools and has side income.
His one worry, **few local lab jobs**, is solved by willingness to move.
He treats AI as an **everyday tool**, not a topic.

steps.text: Keep the supermarket shifts and the gym video work
Learn Python for chemistry data this term
Save a third of my video income each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the second picture. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say bring it on, because writing, checking and planning are exactly what I'm already doing with these tools. I'd tell my gym clients that I can edit videos faster than before, and I'd tell my dad, who is an accountant, to be the person who runs the tools, not the one replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think it's good for me and risky for him. Chemistry still needs people at the bench, and the report-writing and data-checking get quicker. Dad's job is the sort of checking and planning work that software takes first, so I'd worry about his firm laying off juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the tools more deliberately for studying, like making flashcards from lecture slides and checking my code. I'd start charging more for the video work, since I'm faster. I'd also show Dad how I use the tools and suggest he learns the ones for his clients' accounts, so he's the person who runs them, not the one replaced by them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, honestly, with a small stone in my stomach about Dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Dad react if his son told him to learn this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How would Dad react if his son told him to learn this?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the university?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say he's been doing accounts for twenty-five years, and then he'd try it. He's quite curious. I'd show him one task, like sorting receipts, and let him see it works. My mum, who's a nurse, is more worried about robots coming for the hospital, but I'd say that's further off.

I'd tell my accountant dad to **pay attention**.

Dad's checking and planning work is the kind software takes **first**.
do: **Use** the tools deliberately for flashcards and checking code.
**Charge** more for video work now that I'm faster.
**Show** Dad one task, like sorting receipts, so he learns it.
feel: **Excited**, with a small stone in my stomach about Dad.

fieldNote: Felix is **energised** by the change, but his dad's accountancy gives him a real worry.

He raises his **own prices**, reading speed as value.

steps.text: Make flashcards from lecture slides with an AI tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm excited and worried in equal measures, and that two years is crazy fast. I'd post something about learning the tools while we can, and I'd say it to my uni friends over drinks, because we need a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be worried about the household. Dad's accounting work would be done by AI by 2028, and my own degree's data side would be done by AI cheaper than me. Mum, as a nurse, is safer until about 2031, but one wage in the house is hard on a family with me at university.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go full speed. I'd learn as much about the tools as I can, build a freelance business around them, and save every pound. I'd try to start with local firms who'd pay me to set up AI for them. I'd talk to Dad about retraining, and I'd talk to Mum about her savings. And I'd keep the chemistry degree, because a lab is where robots are hardest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit like a rollercoaster. Fast and scary and kind of thrilling, but my stomach drops when I think about home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is freelance work a real plan, or a hope?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Is freelance work a real plan, or a hope?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad about his job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. I've already got two paying clients, so it's real, but it's tiny. I'd need ten before it covers my rent. If it doesn't work, I'd fall back on supermarket shifts and move back home. I'd rather try loudly now than quietly wish later.

say: I'd say I'm **excited and worried** in equal measure, and two years is crazy fast.
I'd tell uni friends to **learn the tools** while we can.
think: Dad's accounting work would be done by AI by **2028**, leaving Mum's nursing wage.
My degree's data side would be done by AI **cheaper** than me.
do: **Build** a freelance business setting up AI tools for local firms.
**Save** every pound and talk to Dad about retraining.
**Keep** the chemistry degree, because labs are where robots are hardest.

S2.quote: I'd rather try loudly now than quietly wish later.
fieldNote: Dad's loss of **accounting income** is the reason for anxiety, not Felix's own prospects.
He answers with **speed and side income**, which fits his adaptive style.

steps.text: Pitch local firms on setting up AI tools for them
Talk to Dad about retraining options

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you start learning now, and I'd say to my friends to pick a skill that mixes tools and hands-on work. I'd say it to Dad over dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd feel good. I'd graduate in 2029, then have about two years before robots take over hands-on work. A mix of chemistry and AI skills would be rare and valuable. Dad would have time to change tracks, and Mum's nursing would last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree with a project that uses machine learning in chemistry. I'd keep the freelance work and grow it slowly. I'd apply for graduate schemes in pharma and for a masters in data-heavy chemistry. And I'd help Dad build a plan for a second income, maybe consulting for small businesses about new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, with a little pressure that keeps me moving. I like that kind of pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change for your dad?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What does the extra time change for your dad?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want in your first job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It changes everything. In two years Dad would be panicking, and in five he can retrain properly, maybe in data work, which he already half does. He'd need to take it seriously by next year, though. Otherwise five years goes quickly.

say: I'd say five years is **plenty** if you start learning now.
I'd tell friends to pick a skill that mixes **tools and hands-on** work.
think: I'd graduate in 2029 with about **two years** before robots take hands-on work.
Chemistry plus AI skills would be **rare and valuable**.

**Apply** for pharma graduate schemes and a data-heavy masters.
**Help** Dad plan a second income, like consulting for small businesses.
feel: **Good**, with a little pressure that keeps me moving.
S3.quote: In two years Dad would be panicking, and in five he can retrain properly, maybe in data work, which he already half does.
fieldNote: Felix's **calm** returns because Dad has time to retrain and Mum's nursing lasts.

He sets a **deadline** for Dad, wanting the family to act by next year.

steps.text: Do a final project using machine learning in chemistry
Help Dad plan consulting work for small businesses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a bonus round, and I'd say people should enjoy it while using the time well. I'd say the best time to learn a new skill is always the year when you don't have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be relaxed. By 2036 I'd be twenty-nine, maybe with a PhD or a job in pharma or a start-up I built. Mum and Dad would be getting close to retirement, so their jobs wouldn't matter as much. I'd be sorry for people who aren't prepared, but I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the degree, then a masters, then try a few years in industry. I'd keep freelancing so I always have a second income. I'd learn programming properly. And I'd put money into an index fund each month, because ten years is a long time for it to grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Easy. It's like looking at a long summer holiday. I'd be curious about what comes next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone with less of a head start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What would you say to someone with less of a head start?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your money look like by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say start with one thing a week. Read one article, try one tool, ask one person who's ahead of you. You don't need a plan, you need a habit. I learned most of what I know by messing around when I should have been revising, and I don't regret it.

I'd say the best time to learn a skill is the year you **don't have to**.

I'd feel sorry for people who aren't **prepared**, but I'd be fine.

**Invest** money in an index fund each month.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, mainly because of Dad. It'd leave him with no time to retrain, and I'd be in the middle of my degree. What would help is quick retraining courses for people his age, tax breaks for learning, and for universities to teach the tools now, not in three years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that not everyone my age is scared. A lot of us find it exciting, but we're also looking after our parents, and that part gets forgotten.

headlineQuote: A lot of us find it exciting, but we're also looking after our parents, and that part gets forgotten.
portrait: Felix is **nineteen**, a chemistry student who stacks supermarket shelves and edits videos for local gyms.
He is **centrist** and adaptive, using AI tools every day and treating them as an everyday toolkit.
His dad is an accountant and his mum a nurse, so the **household worry** is his dad's job.
He is calm in most worlds and **anxious** only when the clock is two years and Dad has no time to retrain.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because Dad would have no time to retrain.
whatWouldHelp: Quick **retraining courses** for people his dad's age, and universities teaching the tools now.
